title: The offer that punishes guessing wrong
subtitle: Part 36 mechanics, acceptance, and the automatic costs consequences of missing the mark
objectives: State the formal requirements of a valid Part 36 offer and the mechanics and time limits governing its acceptance
Explain the automatic costs consequences under CPR 36.17 where a party fails to do better than a Part 36 offer at trial, for both claimant and defendant offers
Explain why Part 36 is deliberately structured to be more punishing than an ordinary without-prejudice settlement offer

leadingAuthorities.role: The self-contained code governing Part 36 offers: form, acceptance, withdrawal and costs consequences
Sets the formal requirements a communication must meet to qualify as a Part 36 offer
Sets the automatic costs consequences that follow where a party fails to beat a Part 36 offer at trial

leadingAuthorities.citation: Gibbon v Manchester City Council [2010] EWCA Civ 726
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms Part 36 is a self-contained procedural code, to be applied on its own terms rather than by analogy with ordinary contract or negotiation principles

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Part 36 is the single most exam-favoured topic in this module, because it rewards mechanical precision — a wrongly counted 21-day period or a misapplied costs consequence changes the whole answer. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the rule exists — this lesson checks whether you can run the numbers on a real offer.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. Expect the test pool to hand you a specific offer, a specific trial outcome, and ask what happens to costs — not just to name the rule.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and get the vocabulary — relevant period, claimant's offer, defendant's offer — solid before the costs-consequence material in Parts 3 and 4, which assumes you already have it.

overview.hook: A claimant is offered £50,000 to settle. They refuse, go to trial, and win — but the judge only awards £45,000. The claimant has technically won the case and still ends up paying the defendant's costs from the date the offer expired, on top of losing their own. That is not a quirk of the system; it is Part 36 working exactly as designed. This lesson is about the mechanism that makes refusing a good offer genuinely dangerous.

parts.heading: What makes an offer a Part 36 offer
parts.voice: structural — builds the formal checklist students will apply throughout
body: Any party can propose settlement terms informally, in a without-prejudice letter, at any time. A Part 36 offer is something more specific: a formal offer made under the Part 36 procedure, which carries its own automatic costs consequences precisely because it follows a strict set of rules. Either a claimant or a defendant can make one, and the mechanics work broadly symmetrically for both, with the costs consequences mirrored depending on who made the offer.

CPR 36.5 sets the formal requirements. To be a valid Part 36 offer, the offer must: be in writing; state that it is intended to have the consequences of Part 36 (a clear statement, not merely a settlement offer that happens to comply in substance); specify a 'relevant period' of not less than 21 days within which the defendant will be liable for the claimant's costs if the offer is accepted; state whether it relates to the whole claim, part of it, or an issue in it; and state whether it takes into account any counterclaim.

That 21-day 'relevant period' is the engine of the whole scheme, so learn it precisely: it is the window during which the offer can be accepted with the costs consequences of ordinary acceptance (essentially, the offeree pays the offeror's costs up to that date) — and it is also the reference point every later costs consequence under CPR 36.17 is measured against.

components.definition: The period, of not less than 21 days, that a Part 36 offer must specify, within which the offer can be accepted without needing the court's permission and the offeree will be liable for the offeror's costs up to that date if accepted. It is the trigger point for the automatic cost consequences under CPR 36.17 if the offer is not beaten at trial.

interaction.prompt: Name the minimum length of the 'relevant period' that a valid Part 36 offer must specify.
interaction.modelAnswer: Not less than 21 days — the offer must give the offeree at least 21 days to accept it under the Part 36 costs regime.

parts.heading: Accepting an offer: the clock and its consequences
parts.voice: practical — walks through the timeline a real case follows
body: Acceptance within the relevant period is straightforward and low-risk: under CPR 36.13, if a Part 36 offer is accepted within the relevant period, the claimant is entitled to its costs of the proceedings up to the date the notice of acceptance was served (where it is the defendant's offer being accepted), and the offeree generally does not need the court's permission to accept.

Acceptance after the relevant period has expired is still possible — a Part 36 offer, once made, remains open for acceptance unless expressly withdrawn — but the costs position shifts: unless the parties agree otherwise, the offeree will typically be liable for the offeror's costs from the end of the relevant period to the date of acceptance, on top of the offeror's costs up to that point being paid in the ordinary way. Late acceptance is not free; it simply trades the risk of an unfavourable trial outcome for a known, but real, costs exposure.

One procedural point trips up candidates: a Part 36 offer can be withdrawn or its terms changed, but only in accordance with CPR 36.9 and 36.10, which generally require serving written notice, and — if the relevant period has not yet expired — obtaining the court's permission is not required to withdraw, but the withdrawal only takes effect from the date of service, not retrospectively. An offer cannot simply be treated as having lapsed because the offeree has gone quiet.

components.title: Accepting a Part 36 offer — the costs consequence path
components.description: A decision path for the costs consequences of accepting a Part 36 offer, depending on timing.

nodes.label: Is the offer accepted within the relevant period?
Yes — offeror recovers costs up to the date of acceptance in the ordinary way, generally without needing court permission
Unless agreed otherwise, offeree generally pays the offeror's costs from the end of the relevant period to the date of late acceptance

components.textAlternative: If a Part 36 offer is accepted within the relevant period, the offeror recovers its costs up to the date of acceptance in the ordinary way. If it is accepted after the relevant period has expired, the offeree will typically also be liable for the offeror's costs from the end of the relevant period to the date of the late acceptance, unless the parties agree otherwise.

interaction.prompt: Put these events in the order they would occur in a case involving late acceptance of a Part 36 offer.
items: Defendant makes a Part 36 offer with a 21-day relevant period
The relevant period expires without acceptance
Six weeks later, the claimant serves notice accepting the offer
The claimant is liable for the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period to the date of acceptance, absent agreement otherwise
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence Part 36 builds in deliberately: the offer stays open, but the cost of waiting accrues from the moment the relevant period closes, not from when the claimant finally decides to accept.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the relevant period must expire first before 'late acceptance' is even possible, and the costs consequence is measured from the end of that period to the date of the eventual acceptance.

parts.heading: Missing your own claimant's offer: the defendant's exposure
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks through a concrete numeric scenario before generalising
body: Now the part of Part 36 that actually decides most litigation strategy: what happens if the case goes to trial instead of settling. CPR 36.17 sets automatic, largely non-discretionary consequences that bite depending on who made the unbeaten offer.

Take a claimant's offer first. Suppose the claimant offers to settle for £40,000, the defendant lets the relevant period expire without accepting, and the case proceeds to trial — where judgment is entered for the claimant at £50,000, a result at least as advantageous to the claimant as its own offer. Under CPR 36.17, unless the court considers it unjust, the claimant is entitled to: interest on the whole or part of the sum awarded at an enhanced rate (up to 10% above base rate) from the end of the relevant period; costs on the indemnity basis from the end of the relevant period; interest on those indemnity costs at the enhanced rate; and an additional amount, calculated as a percentage of the sum awarded (capped, and on a sliding scale set out in the rule), up to a maximum of £75,000.

The defendant, in other words, gambled on trial doing better than £40,000, lost that gamble by £10,000, and now pays a stack of financial penalties on top of the underlying judgment — penalties that exist specifically because Part 36, not an ordinary offer, was on the table.

components.text: Where rule 36.17(1)(b) applies [judgment against the defendant at least as advantageous to the claimant as the claimant's Part 36 offer], the court must, unless it considers it unjust to do so, order that the claimant is entitled to interest on the whole or part of any sum of money awarded at a rate not exceeding 10% above base rate; costs on the indemnity basis from the end of the relevant period; interest on those costs at a rate not exceeding 10% above base rate; and an additional amount, calculated by applying a prescribed percentage to the sum awarded, subject to a maximum of £75,000.
elements: Enhanced interest on damages, up to 10% above base rate
Indemnity costs from the end of the relevant period
Enhanced interest on those indemnity costs
An additional amount on a prescribed sliding scale, capped at £75,000

interaction.prompt: A claimant offers to settle for £40,000 under Part 36. The defendant lets the offer expire and the claimant is awarded £50,000 at trial. What is the starting position under CPR 36.17?
options: Unless the court considers it unjust, the claimant is entitled to enhanced interest, indemnity costs from the end of the relevant period, enhanced interest on those costs, and a capped additional amount
The claimant recovers nothing extra, because the case still went to trial
The defendant automatically recovers its own costs, because it made no offer of its own
The claimant must repay the defendant's costs of trial regardless of the outcome
interaction.explanation: Judgment at £50,000 is at least as advantageous to the claimant as its own £40,000 offer, so CPR 36.17(4) engages: enhanced interest, indemnity costs from the end of the relevant period, enhanced interest on those costs, and the capped additional amount are all in play, subject to the court's residual 'unjust' override.

parts.heading: Missing the defendant's offer: the mirror-image consequence
parts.voice: structural — deliberately parallels Part 3 so students see the symmetry and the difference
body: Now flip the offer. Suppose the defendant offers £50,000 under Part 36, the claimant refuses and lets the relevant period expire, and at trial the claimant is awarded only £45,000 — a result no more advantageous to the claimant than the defendant's offer. Under CPR 36.17(3), unless the court considers it unjust, the claimant will generally be ordered to pay the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, and the defendant's costs will be assessed on the indemnity basis from that date, with interest on those costs at an enhanced rate.

The asymmetry to notice: the defendant does not get the same 'additional amount' penalty the claimant can obtain under CPR 36.17(4) — that particular sanction exists only to protect claimants against a defendant who lowballs and forces a trial, not the other way round. What the defendant does get is the costs-shifting consequence, which on a long-running claim can dwarf the difference between £50,000 and £45,000 many times over, because costs (not just the £5,000 shortfall) are what get reallocated.

The key phrase to hold onto for both directions is 'at least as advantageous' (for a claimant's offer) and 'not more advantageous' (for a defendant's offer, from the claimant's perspective) than the offer — the comparison is always between the actual judgment and the specific offer, not a vague sense of who 'won'.

components.label: CPR 36.17 consequences at a glance
points: Claimant fails to beat a defendant's offer — claimant generally pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, assessed on the indemnity basis, plus enhanced interest on those costs

Defendant fails to beat (i.e. does worse than) a claimant's offer — claimant gets enhanced interest on damages, indemnity costs from the end of the relevant period, enhanced interest on those costs, and a capped additional amount
Both consequences are subject to the court's residual power to depart from them where it would be unjust to apply them, having regard to all the circumstances
The comparison is always judgment vs the specific offer amount — not simply who won the claim overall

interaction.prompt: A defendant offers £50,000 under Part 36. The claimant refuses, goes to trial, and is awarded £45,000. Which of the following is the starting costs position under CPR 36.17(3)?
options: The claimant, having 'won' the claim, automatically recovers all of its costs regardless of the offer
Unless the court considers it unjust, the claimant will generally pay the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, assessed on the indemnity basis, with enhanced interest on those costs
The defendant automatically forfeits its own costs because it made an offer at all
Nothing changes, because Part 36 consequences only ever apply to claimants' offers
interaction.trapExplanation: The trap is equating 'won the claim' with 'did better than the offer'. The claimant recovered damages, but £45,000 is not more advantageous than the £50,000 already on the table, so the Part 36 sanction against the claimant engages — the relevant comparison is judgment vs the specific offer, not simply liability vs no liability.

parts.heading: Why Part 36 bites harder than an ordinary offer
parts.voice: reflective — closes by explaining the design choice, not just the mechanism
body: It is worth pausing on why the rules are built this way, because the reasoning is itself testable. An ordinary without-prejudice settlement offer, if rejected and not beaten at trial, has essentially no automatic costs consequence at all — the general rule that costs follow the event under CPR 44 still applies, and rejecting a good informal offer is not, without more, unreasonable conduct in the Halsey sense covered in the previous lesson.

Part 36 is deliberately engineered to be different: automatic, largely non-discretionary consequences, indemnity (not standard) basis costs, enhanced interest, and — for defendants who lowball claimants — a capped additional financial penalty on top. Gibbon v Manchester City Council underlines why the mechanism has to be applied strictly on its own terms rather than dressed up with contract-law reasoning about offer and acceptance generally: Part 36 is, in the court's words, a self-contained procedural code, and importing outside principles risks undermining the certainty the whole scheme depends on.

That certainty is the point. Because the consequences are close to automatic, both sides can calculate, in advance, exactly what refusing a specific offer will cost if they guess wrong at trial — which is precisely what pushes so many cases that would otherwise go the distance into settlement instead.

components.definition: The characterisation given to Part 36 in Gibbon v Manchester City Council: its rules on offer, acceptance and costs consequences are to be applied as their own complete scheme, not supplemented or displaced by ordinary contract-law principles of offer and acceptance.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that rejecting an ordinary (non-Part 36) without-prejudice settlement offer carries the same automatic costs consequences as rejecting a Part 36 offer?
sliderLabels: Definitely not the same — Part 36 is deliberately more severe
interaction.explanation: Not the same. An ordinary offer has no automatic CPR 36.17-style sanction; at most it may feed into the court's general costs discretion under CPR 44 if refusing it was clearly unreasonable. Part 36's whole design purpose is to impose sharper, largely automatic consequences that an ordinary offer does not carry.

testPool.prompt: Under CPR 36.5, what is the minimum 'relevant period' that a valid Part 36 offer must specify?
options: Not less than 21 days
Not less than 7 days
Not less than 14 days
Not less than 28 days

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is required for a communication to be a valid Part 36 offer under CPR 36.5?
options: It must state that it is intended to have the consequences of Part 36
It must be made orally at a case management hearing
It must be accepted within 7 days or lapse
It must be approved in advance by the court

testPool.prompt: A Part 36 offer's relevant period expires without acceptance. Which of the following best describes the offer's status after that?
options: It remains open for acceptance unless expressly withdrawn, though late acceptance usually carries its own costs consequence
It automatically lapses the moment the relevant period ends
It converts automatically into an ordinary without-prejudice offer with no special status
It can only be revived by making a fresh offer

testPool.prompt: Which case describes Part 36 as a 'self-contained procedural code' that should not be supplemented by ordinary contract-law principles of offer and acceptance?
options: Gibbon v Manchester City Council
Halsey v Milton Keynes General NHS Trust
Unilever plc v The Procter & Gamble Co
PGF II SA v OMFS Company 1 Ltd

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a consequence available to a claimant under CPR 36.17(4) where a defendant fails to beat the claimant's Part 36 offer at trial?
options: Enhanced interest on the sum awarded, up to 10% above base rate
Costs on the indemnity basis from the end of the relevant period
An additional amount calculated on a prescribed scale, capped at £75,000
Automatic committal of the defendant's solicitor for contempt of court
testPool.trapExplanation: Committal is not a Part 36 consequence at all — it belongs to an entirely different area of procedure. The genuine CPR 36.17(4) consequences are financial: enhanced interest, indemnity costs, enhanced interest on those costs, and the capped additional amount.

testPool.prompt: A claimant fails to beat a defendant's Part 36 offer at trial. Which of the following best describes the claimant's exposure under CPR 36.17(3)?
options: The claimant generally pays the defendant's costs from the end of the relevant period, assessed on the indemnity basis, with enhanced interest on those costs
The claimant additionally pays the capped 'additional amount' penalty available under CPR 36.17(4)
The claimant forfeits the entire judgment sum awarded at trial
The claimant is barred from ever bringing a further claim against the same defendant
testPool.trapExplanation: The capped 'additional amount' penalty in option B belongs to the claimant's-offer scenario under CPR 36.17(4), not the defendant's-offer scenario — there is a deliberate asymmetry, and a defendant who beats the claimant's result does not get that extra sum.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best describes the court's power in relation to the CPR 36.17 consequences?
options: The consequences apply unless the court considers it unjust to apply them, having regard to all the circumstances
The consequences are entirely discretionary, with no presumption either way
The consequences can never be departed from, whatever the circumstances
The consequences only apply if both parties consent to Part 36 governing the case
testPool.trapExplanation: The trap is treating the regime as either fully automatic with no override, or fully discretionary. It is neither: the consequences apply by default, and the court has a residual power to depart from them only where applying them would be unjust.

testPool.prompt: A defendant makes a Part 36 offer of £25,000 with a 21-day relevant period. The claimant accepts on day 15. What is the general costs position?
options: The claimant is entitled to its costs of the proceedings up to the date of acceptance, in the ordinary way, without needing the court's permission
The claimant must pay the defendant's costs, because acceptance ends the claimant's cost recovery entirely
Acceptance within the relevant period requires the court's prior permission
No costs order is possible once an offer has been accepted

testPool.prompt: A claimant offers to settle for £60,000 under Part 36. The defendant does not respond, and at trial the claimant is awarded £55,000. Is the CPR 36.17(4) claimant-favourable regime triggered?
options: No — £55,000 is less advantageous to the claimant than its own £60,000 offer, so the claimant did not beat its own offer
Yes — the claimant won the case, so the enhanced consequences automatically apply
Yes — any claimant judgment automatically triggers CPR 36.17(4)
It depends only on whether the defendant responded to the offer at all

testPool.prompt: A defendant's Part 36 offer of £20,000 expires unaccepted. At trial the claimant is awarded £20,000 exactly — not more, not less. Which of the following best captures the relevant comparison under CPR 36.17?
options: Whether the judgment sum is 'at least as advantageous' to the claimant as the offer determines which sanction, if any, applies — an equal result is treated as not beating a defendant's offer for CPR 36.17(3) purposes
Equal results are always treated as a technical win for the claimant, so no sanction applies
Equal results automatically trigger both CPR 36.17(3) and CPR 36.17(4) simultaneously
Part 36 has no application where the figures are identical
testPool.explanation: For a defendant's offer, the claimant needs a result more advantageous than the offer to avoid the CPR 36.17(3) consequences; matching the offer exactly does not count as beating it, so the claimant's costs exposure from the end of the relevant period is engaged, subject to the court's discretion.

testPool.prompt: A claimant wants to withdraw a Part 36 offer before the relevant period has expired. What must the claimant do?
options: Serve written notice of withdrawal in accordance with the Part 36 rules; the withdrawal takes effect from the date of service, not retrospectively
Simply stop referring to the offer, which is treated as an implied withdrawal
Obtain the defendant's written consent before any withdrawal can take effect
Nothing — a Part 36 offer cannot be withdrawn once made

testPool.prompt: Under CPR 36.17(4), the capped 'additional amount' a claimant may recover where a defendant fails to beat the claimant's offer is subject to a maximum of which figure?
options: There is no cap at all

testPool.prompt: Under CPR 36.17, on what basis are costs generally assessed where the relevant Part 36 sanction is triggered, in contrast to the standard basis that usually applies?
options: The indemnity basis
The fixed costs basis
The small claims track basis
There is no special basis — costs remain on the standard basis

testPool.prompt: A Part 36 offer is accepted after the relevant period has expired, and the parties have not agreed costs between themselves. What is the default costs position under Part 36 for the period after the relevant period ended?
options: The offeree will generally be liable for the offeror's costs from the end of the relevant period to the date of the late acceptance
The offeror automatically loses its right to recover any costs at all
Costs are assessed exclusively by reference to the trial date, even though there was no trial
No costs order can be made where an offer is accepted late

testPool.prompt: Under CPR 36.5, which of the following must a valid Part 36 offer state, in addition to specifying the relevant period?
options: Whether it relates to the whole claim, part of it, or a specific issue, and whether it takes into account any counterclaim
The offeror's assessment of its own litigation risk in percentage terms
The identity of the trial judge expected to hear the case
The exact date on which trial is listed to begin

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is conflating 'who won the claim' with 'who beat the offer'. Part 36's comparison is always judgment vs the specific offer figure — a claimant can win damages and still be sanctioned, and a defendant can lose the claim and still trigger a claimant-favourable sanction, depending purely on where the trial figure landed relative to the offer.
